newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT - Coaching next step for retiring Patel.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT - Coaching next step for retiring Patel.

text.p: WELLINGTON, July 16 - New Zealand offspinner Dipak Patel announced his retirement from international cricket on Wednesday and said he faced a bigger challenge in his new ambition of making his mark as a coach.
The 38-year-old stepped down against the wishes of the national selectors and coach Steve Rixon.
Patel cited family commitments, the pressures of long tours and his sated appetite for international cricket in his decision to quit.
"I sat down with the family and made my decision over the last month," he told NZPA.
"The selectors wanted me to make myself available for another season, particularly when you consider the tour of Australia at the end of the year and the very tough nature of playing there.

"I spoke to Ross Dykes (convener of selectors) and he was keen to try and convince me to stay on for one last season, but I didn't think I could commit myself mentally and physically for such a long season away with tours to Zimbabwe and Australia."

Patel said while he felt physically fine to continue, at the back of his mind he was concerned about the possibility of breaking down, particularly in Australia where scrutiny on and off the field is relentless.
"The knee and hamstrings are well at the moment, but I don't know if they would last the distance of such a long summer."
He said his family were keen for him to continue for another season if he had chosen to do so.
"They enjoyed being part of the set-up, the atmosphere and being around the game," Patel said.
"But after 22 years of first class cricket and 10 years of international cricket I think I've had a very good innings.
"I'm grateful that I was allowed 10 years of international cricket. It would probably have never happened if I had stayed in England."
Kenyan-born and English-bred, Patel moved to New Zealand in 1985 after being enticed here by former New Zealand captain and master batsman Martin Crowe.
His last international appearance was in India in May when New Zealand were eliminated after the preliminary stages of the Independence Cup one-day tournament, won by World Cup holders Sri Lanka.
He has played 37 tests for New Zealand, scoring 1200 runs at an average of 20.68 with a highest score of 99 (against England) and taking 75 wickets at 42.05.
He has played 75 one-day internationals, scoring 623 runs and taking 45 wickets, conceding an average of 4.14 runs per over.
He has scored 15,188 runs in 358 first-class matches, 236 of them at county level in England.
Only six New Zealand players -- Glenn Turner, John Wright, Martin Crowe, Bert Sutcliffe, Geoff Howarth and John Reid -- have scored more runs at first-class level.
Having made his decision to retire, he was now keen to prove himself just as good as a coach, if not better, he said.
Already he has had feelers from Kenya and other non-test playing nations as well as approaches from provinces within New Zealand.
New Zealand Cricket officials, including coach Steve Rixon and operations manager John Reid, are among those who are keen for him to take up a role in this country.

Rixon has told him that while he felt his philosophy on the game and the way it is played was well balanced, his principal attribute was his ability to generate camaraderie and rapport, particularly with the younger players.
Teenage spinner Daniel Vettori is one who will vouch for that, Patel having taken the youngster firmly under his wing and guided his introduction at international level.
"I've had a lot of encouragement to get into coaching, they (NZC administration and management) seem to think that I'd make a good fist of it," he said.
"After playing for this long it would seem a shame to walk away from it all and not put anything back."
He said he viewed coaching as a more encompassing role than playing.
"Coaching is a huge challenge, it's about man-management, getting these young guys to believe in themselves and those around them, and giving them the right sort of encouragement," Patel said.
"I think the most important thing is knowing, or learning what to do as a coach when the heads go down, and how to get those players mentally up again.
"Cricket is essentially a mental game and preparing players for that is really the challenge, so I think it is a natural progression for me to go into that side of the game."
Patel said he would spend the next few weeks savouring his memories of the game and his achievements.

He insisted that he didn't want to dwell on any particular moments, but when pressed conceded that the 1992 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand where he opened the bowling in a shock move by captain Crowe and coach Warren Lees was probably his finest hour.
"If you pointed to any one particular moment in my career I think that would be it," he said.
